Chapter 3: METHODOLOGY (p. 48) details a 'two-phase research exploration' including a 'survey' sent to 'professional organizations' and 'individuals'.
The survey consisted of 'biophilic attributes designed into several series of various conceptual restorative healing environment digital renderings' (p. 18, 50).
'Quantitative data was collected... Qualitative data was also collected to glean a deeper understanding...' (p. 59).
Chapter 4: FINDINGS (p. 57) presents quantitative and qualitative results from the survey.
Chapter 6: DESIGN SOLUTION (p. 122) applies the research findings to a specific architectural design project.

limitations: Data not modeled for other areas of nature-driven design (sustainable/environmental design). (p. 20, 54)
Study did not investigate biophilic design perception outside alternative healthcare and restorative settings. (p. 20, 55)
Generalization to other types of healthcare environments may not be warranted. (p. 21, 55)
Data analysis focused solely on specified biophilic elements in a restorative healing environment, excluding others from the developed framework. (p. 20, 54)
Participants were shown only three digital renderings per biophilic attribute, representing only one view of a larger, three-dimensional space. (p. 54)
Data collected was based on perception of digital renderings, not physical experience/occupation of spaces. (p. 54)
Design solution was for a building in a dense urban environment. (p. 55)
Design excluded biophilic attributes deemed unachievable due to building size, geographic location, or physical adjacencies in its urban context. (p. 55)
Generalization to other urban built environments was not warranted for the design. (p. 55)
Framework included only nine of 70+ biophilic design attributes due to time constraints, limiting surveyed and emphasized attributes. (p. 168)
Potential argument that chosen biophilic attributes may not be the most vital based on personal perception. (p. 168)
Small sample size may limit significance of data for accurate depiction of professional perceptions. (p. 173)
Inability to survey potential clients, only professionals involved in design/work within the space. (p. 173-174)
minimum_safe_summary: This thesis investigates the perceived effectiveness of biophilic design attributes in urban restorative healing environments to inform a design solution for a wellness resort. A mixed-methods approach, including a survey of design and alternative healthcare professionals, revealed that transitional spaces maximizing sightlines and accessibility to the exterior were preferred for promoting exploration. Expansive, overhead natural lighting with views to natural settings was favored for evoking reverence and spirituality. Inside-outside spaces offering protection from elements while maintaining high visibility were seen as most effective for prospect and refuge. Large-scale, active water features and expansive, eye-level living greenery were perceived to best promote a sense of change and metamorphosis due to their dynamic visual and auditory qualities. Limitations include a small sample size, reliance on 2D renderings, and a restricted set of biophilic attributes, which may affect the generalizability of the findings to other contexts or user groups.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural or biophilic environments can restore directed attention capacity.
Exposure to natural or biophilic environments can reduce physiological and psychological stress.

mechanism_chain.description: Biophilic design elements, such as those found in transitional spaces, lead to a perception of naturalness, openness, and mystery. This perception engages involuntary attention and fosters a sense of exploration and discovery, which in turn contributes to restorative experiences and overall well-being.
